In Ch’ttahh , Bilal El Had returns to the dance form of his youth: Moroccan Chaabi, the popular dance and folk music inextricably linked to weddings, living room parties, and street celebrations. The piece intertwines contemporary dance with the centuries-old rhythms, songs, and symbols of Chaabi. Through a play of gestures, El Had explores the long history of men challenging gender conventions in dance, poetry, or music.

By exposing the disruption of conventional masculinity inherent in Chaabi, Bilal El Had allows echoes from the archive to collide with contemporary bodies. In doing so, he demonstrates through choreography how social norms are embodied, enforced, and defied. The transformative potential of the dance surfaces, via the expressive intensity of Chaabi, to preserve cultural memory and, simultaneously, to cautiously chart a course for the future.

Between tribute and renewal, humour and indictment, Ch’ttahh channels the explosiveness of the present, to cast a loving glance at a collective past.

Bilal El Had (b. 1991) is a Moroccan dancer and performer who lives and works in Brussels. After training at P.A.R.T.S., he has collaborated as a performer with (among others) Anne Teresa De Keersmaeker, Salva Sanchis, Radouan Mriziga, Laurent Chétouane, and Maud Blandel.

La Parabole du Seum is an attempt to survive.

An attempt that begins on the margins, from life experiences that resist the norm, and how that norm crushes us.

In the light of rising fascism (and the fascism that is already among us), Rébecca Chaillon offers neither a program nor consolation. She shares an experience: that of people struggling with a world that’s too big, too heavy, too urgent, despite their longing for lightness.

Between heaven and earth, the rooftops of Seine-Saint-Denis (department 93) house satellite dishes aimed at a distant place that is full, fragmented, and already occupied. A place marked by French colonial history, by the neglect of public services and organized marginalization, but also by strategies for living that are constantly inventing new techniques of survival.

Confronted with materialistic rationality and the monotheistic norms of power and purity, religious syncretism, hybrid beliefs, and secular rituals function as methods of poetic and political resistance, ways to let the soul breathe.

In La Parabole du seum , heaven is both the place from which disasters strike (hurricanes, floods, so-called ‘natural’ disasters, which always uncover the same fault lines and divisions) and the new territories of Western imperialism.

If the sky is raging and no longer empty, what space remains to project our beliefs onto?

The body is a fleeting place of discourse: it is a place where we create, unravel, and transform meaning via movement. How do our bodies speak, how do we decipher an abundance of signs? And what role does language play in this? Mercury Rising explores the slippery nature of interpretation, and ultimately liberates us from the necessity of the literal, the explanatory.

The performance examines language in a direct, phenomenological manner. With makers and performers Dawn Jani Birley, Rita Mazza, and Lukas Malkowski, Jefta van Dinther maps out both ancient and future non-linear languages. Together, they navigate a terrain on which communication, gestures, agency, and corporeality can intersect.

Incorporating multiple sign languages and created for all audiences, including both deaf and hearing spectators, the work addresses the complexity of human communication on the brink of a paradigm shift. What we ultimately share is not certainty, but the impossibility of fully understanding each other, and the urge to connect nonetheless.

• Jefta van Dinther (Sweden/Germany) is a choreographer and dancer. His work is characterized by a rigorous, physical approach and always implies a staged investigation of movement itself. The moving body forms the core of his practice, but belongs to and interacts with a body of light, sound, and materials. Central to his work is the question: what does it mean to be human?

Trying Things Out is an evening that offers a glimpse into two performance works that are still very much in development. There is no “premiere pressure”; instead, attention, curiosity, and care take center stage. The audience is invited to discover what is still being researched, shaped, questioned, and experimented with, and to engage in an informal conversation with the makers afterwards.

In recent years, Globe Aroma has welcomed several performing artists who are looking for artistic companionship, rehearsal space, coaching, technical support, and a network within the sector. With Trying Things Out, we are building a gentle in-between step between studio and audience, a testing ground where makers are given time, space, and a community to try out their work, fail, grow, and learn together. It is not a show. It is a moment in the process. A place where watching is a form of care, and feedback is a gift.

Come watch, listen, share.

Béatrice Meguem TAXIWOMAN

With TAXIWOMAN , Béatrice explores the place society assigns to women and the way it looks at those who do not fit the mould. The project speaks of resilience and starting over somewhere else: in a place that thinks differently and offers better possibilities.

The performance lasts approximately 30 minutes.

• Béatrice Meguem is an actress, storyteller and project manager. With more than fifteen years of experience, she places the power of live art at the heart of her practice.

Under the weight of the genocide in Gaza, sleep has become a stolen respite for bodies living under constant psychological pressure and fear, beneath fragile tents struggling to withstand shelling and artillery fire. By keeping the sounds of explosions present around the clock, the colonisers deliberately keep people in a state of perpetual terror and anticipation, seeking to shatter their sense of safety and turn the land to which they belong into a place where life becomes unbearable.

With Sleep , Hamada Elkept attempts to convey to an Europen audience what it means for people to sleep during the genocide, after losing their homes, their beds, and the moments of safety that once allowed them to close their eyes without fear.

In our daily lives, we rarely think about where, how, or when we will sleep. For us, sleep is something we take for granted. Yet this installation, through its stories, reveals a profound human divide and speaks of privilege and inequality.

Sleep invites us to listen to a reality in which the night has become another spectre haunting human life, and the act of sleeping itself has turned into a daily struggle to reclaim a moment of rest amid constant fear.

13 years in the making. Finally on vinyl.

It’s happening! After 13 years, countless performances and an impressive repertoire of songs, the time has finally come: buren are releasing their long-awaited LP!

Oshin Albrecht & Melissa Mabesoone present buren Greatest Hits, a compilation of their favourite, most iconic and most unforgettable songs, produced by Benne Dousselaere.

From ‘Have you rearranged the flowers?’ (2014) to ‘Blue Skies Forever’ (2018), from ‘SPARE TIME WORK’ (2021) to ‘shoe/farm – prelude’ (2023) and ‘shoe/farm – a family business’ (2025): more than five shows, thirteen years of buren and a selection of absolute bangers. Including, amongst others, ‘This Is The Picture’, ‘Picture This’, ‘Mr. Rabbit’, ‘Cinderella Story’, ‘Potato Song’ and ‘Buffaloes for the teens’, ‘Pumps made of jeans’.

Do you know them all? Then this is the night for you. Don’t know them yet? Then this is the perfect moment to get to know them. For the fans, the newcomers, the die-hards and the casual sing-alongs: this won’t be just any album launch, but a proper neighbours’ celebration.

Expect an evening where everyone can grab the mic and belt out the ‘Buren’ classics at the top of their lungs. There’ll be a KARAOKE BOOT!

Dress code? GLITTER & GLAM. Come dressed as your favourite ‘Buren’ character, straight out of your favourite show. Think bigger, bolder, shinier. Sequins, drama, glamour, over-the-top looks: anything goes, nothing is too much.

The interactive series Wonders of Multilingualism is a collaboration between Kaaitheater and Passa Porta. Previous editions have explored themes such as language and identity, comfort, migration, power, and language acquisition or mother tongue. This eighth and final edition, with the theme ‘Multilingual Dutch’ (Meertalig Nederlands), focuses on how a multilingual society enriches the Dutch language.

A multilingual society constantly enriches the Dutch language with new stories, words and sounds. Writers Tessa Leuwsha, Mira Bryssinck and Lisetta Ma Neza each pay tribute to ‘Multilingual Dutch’ (Meertalig Nederlands), in pieces written especially for this programme. Academic Hari Prasad Sacré offers a guide to understanding and supporting the renewal of the Dutch language. He explains how ‘Multilingual Dutch’ (Meertalig Nederlands) emerged from experiences of migration and continued to evolve through stories about gender and disability.

An evening where you can journey from Suriname to Brussels, whether you’re a long-time or a new speaker of Dutch. Connect with the Dutch language as it tells underrepresented stories about the past, present and future. The evening will feature music by jazz musician Peter Somuah.

This programme is curated by Hari Prasad Sacré. At the invitation of Kaaitheater and Passa Porta, Hari developed this programme around his keynote speech ‘Multilingual Dutch’ (Meertalig Nederlands).

The exhibition Faces of Where I Am From presents a selection of recent and newly produced works by Palestinian, Brussels-based artist Hussein Shamia .

Combining large-scale paintings with small drawings and watercolours, Shamia invites viewers to engage with questions that remain ever-present in his experience of displacement: the longing for his motherland, the act of remembering, and the desire to remain connected to those who have stayed under occupation, by choice or by force.

Shamia reflects on how the violence of occupation and siege transforms familiar faces — those of family members and people from the neighbourhood — into unrecognisable ones. Individual features and personal traits gradually disappear beneath a veil of suffering, despair, and pain. Reduced to robotic entities forced to follow the system in order to survive, people somehow become indistinguishable from one another, yet each carries a different story.

Faces and bodies become mirrors of a page of history that remains painfully open, yet is often forgotten amid the noise of daily life. Faces of Where I Am From becomes a space for remembrance and acknowledgment, bringing these faces and the stories they carry back into focus.

Agenda 4/12 (open until 22:00) 17:30 Exhibition opening Beursschouwburg + welcome drink 18:15 Artist talk: Hussein Shamia in conversation with moderator Özge Akarsu. Limited capacity – please arrive on time!

Take a peek behind the scenes of the artistic workplace at Globe Aroma, where the magic happens. On the first floor, artists create, experiment, rehearse, and inspire one another every day. This is where ideas become tangible: sketches grow into paintings, fabrics into costumes, and words into performances.

Usually, the work in the atelier happens behind closed doors, in the quiet of the evenings or amid the hustle and bustle of everyday life. But from time to time, it’s time for artists to branch out, welcome new perspectives, and plant the seeds for conversations, exchanges, and perhaps even collaborations.

Surrounded by artworks and the living process of making, we bring artists, audiences, and cultural professionals together in one shared space, over a drink.

Think of it as something in between a studio visit, a networking moment, and a drink among friends.

Participating artists: Hussein Shamia, Hamada Elkept, Ismail Matar, Tatiana7elementart, SHADE

Curated by Tijani , the closing party brings together a rich mix of West African sounds, musical traditions and contemporary influences. Featuring the soulful Peul flute and percussion of Issa Ndour , the traditional Fulani music and reggae fusion of Fouta Flow , and an eclectic DJ set by DJ Allabai , blending reggae, dancehall, Afro, house and musical gems from the Senegambia region.

An evening of rhythm, cultural exchange and celebration.

• Issa Ndour is a flutist and djembe and kora drummer. He began playing the djembe at the age of seven and the Peul flute (“tokhoro”) at eleven, studying with Baye Cheikh and Fallou Sy in Thiès, Senegal.

He started his musical career performing at weddings and went on to collaborate with numerous Senegalese groups, including Ben Bopp and Waflash, as well as international musicians such as American percussionist Tony Vacca and Swedish musician Ali Muller. He has also contributed to a large number of music albums.

Since 2012, he has been a Peul flute and djembe musician with the National Ballet of the Daniel Sorano National Theatre in Dakar. He has represented Senegal on numerous international tours, performing in countries including China, Turkey, Italy, Germany and Tunisia.

• Fouta Flow — “the voice of a villager” in the Pulaar language of West Africa — is a musical project blending traditional music and reggae. It was initiated by Zakaria Bocoum, a Mauritanian singer, songwriter and composer.

Chris-Armel Iradukunda Rêves lucides d’une santé sans papiers

In this performance, Chris-Armel Iradukunda invites the audience to take part in a theatrical simulation based on a future scenario for healthcare for undocumented people in Brussels.

What if people who have been overlooked by the healthcare system for years could have their medical expenses reimbursed and collectively manage a solidarity fund that supplements the emergency medical aid provided by the Belgian state? How might such an initiative work?

Five years ago, Dorothée Munyaneza met Christian Nka for the first time in the Foresta Park in Marseille’s Quartiers Nord. Christian is a former boxing champion and a local legend who has never left his neighbourhood. He radiates immense power, with his tall body, large hands, and full beard. And wisdom.

Three years after their first meeting, Christian and Dorothée decide to create a performance together. He speaks freely about his childhood, his parents, and the violence that has marked his life on the margins of society, but against which he also rebels. He teaches her boxing moves, looking out at the sea. And he dances.

The composer Ben LaMar Gay (with whom Dorothée has often collaborated) created the music for the performance. A portrait of Christian Nka emerges through his notes and words – an unflinching portrait that questions what masculinity, violence, and fatherhood (and what we inherit of all these things and what we pass on) can mean.

• Choreographer, writer, musician, and artistic director Dorothée Munyaneza (Kigali, 1982) is developing a passionate oeuvre. Starting from reality, she aims to capture memory and the body, carry the voices of those we silence, give heed to the silences, and reveal the scars of history. Munyaneza has previously appeared at Kaaitheater with Mailles , Toi , Moi... Tituba , Umuko , and Inconditionnelles .

Khadija El Kharraz Alami draws inspiration for her immersive theatre performance SHRINE from the work of feminist activist Silvia Federici. In her essay Caliban and the Witch , Federici describes the role of women in the context of the transition to capitalism, and in particular the witch hunts that so marked this period. She also points out the impact of these patriarchal practices on social structures that still exist today.

SHRINE relies on a story (but above all a pattern, a narrative structure) of a Daughter who seeks refuge with the Djinns , non-human beings, in a world parallel to our own. She, a Daughter, who carries the greatest pain, sorrow, and grief, is wanted by the government. Her mother was brutally murdered by the systems maintained by humans and powers. The Daughter bears witnesses to this and chooses a fair fight for justice, following the steps of the rule of law.

El Kharraz Alami demonstrates once again how she can transform essayistic work into action, and how she finds forms that make the role of the marginalized woman in our societies tangible. How this leads to alienation and social inequality, and how the struggle for radical equality defines one's position in society. Which erased roles of women in societies can we revive, and which buried cries will be heard?

Tilted between a lawsuit and a mourning process, Alami hits her mark with ‘Shrine’ when she lets go of the mythological world of the Djinns and stands in the middle of the room.

20:30–22:00 SAWT (DJ set)

With an ambient soundscape that unfolds gradually, SAWT sets the mood for the evening. Blending atmospheric textures and subtle rhythms, his set creates a space to drift, connect and ease into the music.

SAWT is the musical alias of Kamel Badarneh, a Palestinian electronic music artist. Working with experimental electronics, he moves away from traditional instruments, creating soundscapes through urban field recordings and MIDI controllers. His sets are rich in atmosphere, leaving a resonance that lingers long after the performance.

22:00 Quarter Tone, Hussein Rassim, IM’IN (live concert)

Quarter Tone, Hussein Rassim and IM’IN bring their distinct musical worlds together in a live concert. Moving between Arabic musical traditions, experimental sounds and contemporary electronic influences, they create a shared soundscape where different rhythms, voices and musical practices meet.

Hala El Moussawi (Quarter Tone) works at the intersection of voice, research and storytelling. With Quarter Tone, she draws on the Arabic maqamat she sings in, exploring states of grief, resistance, belonging and displacement. With a background in social geography and migration studies, she approaches music as a form of research. Through vocal experimentation, field recordings and sonic imagination, she translates personal and collective memory into sound.

Hussein Rassim is an Iraqi musician based in Brussels, specialising in the oud (oriental lute).

The documentary Moeder Suriname – Mama Sranan offers us a glimpse into the colonial past through the eyes of a Surinamese laundress. Filmmaker Tessa Leuwsha brings to life the stories of Surinamese women, such as her grandmother, through a wealth of impressive and, in some cases, colourised archive footage.

Multilingual Dutch embraces not only new words or expressions, but also new and under-represented experiences from our shared history and world. Through this film, you will see and discover how the Dutch language carries more stories than we often realise. Through the eyes of a Surinamese laundress, we look at our shared history – and at ourselves – in a different light.

Synopsis: Mama Sranan

She was born in 1905 in a hamlet to a white mother and a black father – a disgrace. Her father is forced to leave, and her mother also disappears. She herself is taunted as a half-breed, does not attend school, and quickly discovers the reality of colonial power dynamics (“we work and they watch”). She has a child, whose father is always away working for the Dutch, and moves to Paramaribo, where she has three more children whom she raises on her own.

Meanwhile, she sees national self-awareness growing. But when all her children move to the Netherlands even before Suriname’s independence in 1975, she follows them, with a heavy heart. She does not settle there: “In Holland, paradise is like a shadow, just ahead or behind you.

In the workshop Artificial Intelligence7 , artist Tatiana Zubieta, who works under the name Tatiana7elementart , invites participants to create masks using recycled materials and everyday objects, including functional items. By transforming and combining these materials, we will give them a new life, turning familiar objects into something else.

Artificial Intelligence7 explores the relationship between technology, identity, materiality, and the digital world. Each material carries an archaeology of meanings and uses, shaped by its past and the different stages of its life. Every discarded object carries traces of its previous life, which we can uncover, reinterpret, and transform through the act of assembling them together. By giving these objects new forms and meanings, we can use the masks to express something about themselves, explore different aspects of their identity, or imagine who they might become.

• Brussels-based, Colombian-born Tatiana7elementart is a multidisciplinary artist exploring the physicality of materials and their transformation through means of sculpture, video, photo, installation, and collage. Zubieta uses industrial equipment (metal, engines or wires) as source material, repurposed for her work: at the core of her artistic practice is the transformation of recycled and found materials, as opposed to the extraction and exploitation that the use of new materials requires.

On December 5, ECOPOLIS, Fair(er) Futures Festival will once again bring together thinkers and doers, writers, artists, and activists from various countries for a day filled with inspiring conversations, hopeful ideas, and new perspectives.

After all, we live in a time of great challenges : think of climate disruption and growing inequality. This raises numerous questions. How do we build a future that works for everyone again? And what do we need to envision—and also shape—that future?

We ask the big questions—such as the one posed by Anna Tsing : What is the art of living on a damaged planet? Questions that have become all too real in the face of extreme heat waves and wildfires. And they show that, ultimately, this is a matter of justice —not only here but also in the Global South. Because those who contribute the least to ecological disruption are hit the hardest. Nepal is a painful example of this. And that’s what we need to talk about.

That’s why ECOPOLIS remains a place to stimulate your imagination and push boundaries. Because only if we can imagine a better society can we shape it.

Archive of Potential Loss

Over the past fifty years, wild animal populations have shrunk by almost three-quarters on average, mainly due to the way the wealthy world produces and consumes. What was once commonplace is becoming increasingly rare, and because we never experienced it, we forget how abundant all other life was not so long ago.

In Ch’ttahh , Bilal El Had returns to the dance form of his youth: Moroccan Chaabi, the popular dance and folk music inextricably linked to weddings, living room parties, and street celebrations. The piece intertwines contemporary dance with the centuries-old rhythms, songs, and symbols of Chaabi. Through a play of gestures, El Had explores the long history of men challenging gender conventions in dance, poetry, or music.

By exposing the disruption of conventional masculinity inherent in Chaabi, Bilal El Had allows echoes from the archive to collide with contemporary bodies. In doing so, he demonstrates through choreography how social norms are embodied, enforced, and defied. The transformative potential of the dance surfaces, via the expressive intensity of Chaabi, to preserve cultural memory and, simultaneously, to cautiously chart a course for the future.

Between tribute and renewal, humour and indictment, Ch’ttahh channels the explosiveness of the present, to cast a loving glance at a collective past.

Bilal El Had (b. 1991) is a Moroccan dancer and performer who lives and works in Brussels. After training at P.A.R.T.S., he has collaborated as a performer with (among others) Anne Teresa De Keersmaeker, Salva Sanchis, Radouan Mriziga, Laurent Chétouane, and Maud Blandel.

In this workshop, visual artist SHADE invites participants to explore collage as a tool for self-expression and a way to explore and re/construct identity. By deconstructing existing imagery — vintage prints, personal photos, printed matters and social media visuals — we will learn how memories, perception, and personal stories can be reassembled into new visual narratives to ‘narrate ourselves’.

Through hands-on experimentation with textures, layers, and composition, we’ll play with themes of identity, memory, and transformation, discovering how apparently unrelated fragments can come together to create personal (or collective) portraits.

• SHADE is a Belgium-based visual artist born in Russia. Working across analog collage, photography, and mixed media, his practice investigates the intersections of memory, bodily transformation, loss, and queer identity. With a background in photography, SHADE merges personal archives with found vintage print media, exploring how human identity and emotions are continuously fragmented, reinterpreted, and reconstructed. As an educator and artist, he approaches collage as an “intuitive laboratory”: a tactile medium for visual storytelling, self-exploration, and personal narrative building. His work has been presented in cultural spaces including Beursschouwburg (Brussels), the Belgian Poster Festival (Antwerp), The Village (Berlin).

Who’s Cooking (for Whom)?

A food performance and public conversation on how the design of a kitchen can shape and transform the relationship between host and guest.

Who is cooking for whom? Who is the host, and who is the guest?

As part of The House for Collective Imagination*, Globe Aroma invites you to Who’s Cooking (for Whom)? , a participatory dinner and public conversation exploring the design of its new kitchen through questions of hospitality and shared ownership.

The dinner is part of a longer co-creative process around the design of Globe Aroma’s new kitchen. Since March 2026, weekly community lunches at Globe Aroma have brought people together to experiment with different ways of hosting, sharing food and making others feel welcome. These experiences raise questions about how a kitchen can accommodate different ways of using and sharing a space: from cooking a meal for yourself or inviting friends over for dinner, to preparing collective meals or welcoming an audience during public events.

But who is cooking for whom? Who serves the food, and who is being served? Who has paid to be here, and who hasn’t? Who speaks to whom? And what do these different roles tell us about hospitality? During this participatory dinner, we invite you to explore these questions through the experience of sharing a meal. Rather than simply attending a food performance, you will take an active part in it.
